_meta.purpose: Our own one-line description of every technical syllabus item, per level. The RSGB owns the wording of the learning objectives, so nothing here is copied from them. These are what a bench displays as its subject line.
_meta.voice: Measured from G0LFT's published RadCom articles: median 14-15 words, roughly a third under 12, second person, colons not semicolons, no em dashes.
_meta.syllabus: Syllabus 2019 per-level specifications v1.5, cross-checked against combined v1.6b

2A1.foundation: Current is electrons on the move. Which everyday materials let them through, and which do not.
2A1.intermediate: Components are never exactly their marked value. Every one carries a tolerance.
2A1.full: How tolerances add up across a circuit, and what that does to the result you get.

2A2.foundation: Current needs a complete loop and something to push it. How it splits, and how it does not.

2B1.foundation: Power in watts, and why a resistor carrying current warms up.
2B1.full: Finding current, voltage, resistance and power anywhere in a series or parallel network.

2C1.foundation: Resistance opposes current. How voltage, current and resistance tie together.
2C1.intermediate: Resistors and cells in series and parallel, and solving for whichever quantity you are missing.

2C2.foundation: The voltages across resistors in series add up to the supply voltage.
2C2.intermediate: Two or three resistors as a potential divider, and how to work out the output.

2C3.intermediate: EMF and potential difference are not the same thing. Draw current, and the source sags.

2C4.foundation: Getting the polarity right, and what happens when you get it wrong.

2D1.intermediate: What a capacitor is made of, and how it holds a charge.
2D1.full: What sets the value: plate area, plate spacing, and the dielectric between them.

2D2.intermediate: Combining capacitors in series and in parallel.
2D2.full: Why different dielectrics suit different jobs, and how their losses grow with frequency.

2D3.intermediate: Some capacitors are polarised. Connect one backwards and it can hurt you.
2D3.full: Every capacitor has a voltage it will not survive.

2D4.intermediate: Move a conductor through a magnetic field and you induce a voltage across it.
2D4.full: Self-inductance, and the back EMF a coil throws out when its current changes.

2D5.intermediate: Combining inductors in series and in parallel.

2D6.intermediate: What makes a coil's inductance larger: more turns, wider diameter, closer spacing, and the core.

2D7.full: How current and voltage rise and fall in LR and CR circuits, and what the time constant tells you.

2E1.foundation: Direct current flows one way. Alternating current keeps changing direction.
2E1.intermediate: A capacitor charges and discharges each way, so it passes AC but blocks DC.

2E2.foundation: The sine wave as a picture of AC, and the frequencies radio works at.
2E2.intermediate: Reading amplitude and frequency off a sine wave, and how period and frequency relate.

2E3.intermediate: In a resistor, voltage and current stay in step. What RMS means and why it is used.
2E3.full: Current lags voltage in an inductor and leads it in a capacitor. Working out reactance.

2E4.intermediate: Capacitive reactance, and why it falls as the frequency climbs.
2E4.full: Using a capacitor to couple a signal through, or to send it to ground.

2E5.intermediate: Inductive reactance, and why it rises as the frequency climbs.
2E5.full: Using an inductor to block AC while letting DC pass.

2E6.intermediate: Put resistance and reactance together and the circuit both stores energy and loses it as heat.
2E6.full: Impedance as resistance and reactance combined, and working it out for a series CR or LR circuit.

2E7.foundation: How frequency and wavelength relate, and the units each one uses.
2E7.intermediate: Using v = f x wavelength to get from one to the other.

2E8.intermediate: On a wire as long as the wave it carries, current and voltage differ from one end to the other.

2F1.foundation: An analogue signal changes smoothly. A digital one is a stream of samples.
2F1.intermediate: More bits and faster sampling give you a closer copy of the original.
2F1.full: Sample too slowly and a signal turns up at the wrong frequency entirely.

2F2.foundation: What an analogue to digital converter does, and why you need something to process the result.
2F2.full: The Fourier transform, which turns a signal in time into a picture of its frequencies.

2G1.intermediate: Two coils sharing one magnetic field, and what the core is there for.
2G1.full: Turns ratio sets voltage and current. Square it and you have the impedance ratio.

2H1.intermediate: An inductor and capacitor together make a tuned circuit. At one frequency their reactances match.
2H1.full: Finding the resonant frequency, or the L or C you need to land on one.

2H2.intermediate: At resonance a series circuit shows low impedance and a parallel one shows high impedance.
2H2.full: A crystal behaves like a tuned circuit, with a series and a parallel resonance close together.

2H3.intermediate: Energy swaps back and forth between capacitor and coil. Larger values give a lower frequency.

2H4.intermediate: Selectivity, and how the bandwidth compares with the frequency at the centre of it.
2H4.full: Q as magnification. The voltages inside a tuned circuit can dwarf the one you put in.

2H5.intermediate: Low pass, high pass, band pass and notch filters, and the shape each response takes.
2H5.full: Dynamic resistance, and what it means at resonance.

2I1.intermediate: A diode conducts one way only, once you give it enough forward voltage to start.
2I1.full: A Zener diode conducts backwards once you pass its rated voltage, and holds there.

2I2.intermediate: A varicap works as a capacitor whose value you set with the reverse voltage.

2I3.intermediate: A small base current steers a much larger collector current. That is where the gain comes from.
2I3.full: Biasing bipolar transistors and FETs so they sit where you want them.

2I4.intermediate: The common emitter amplifier, and picking the collector resistor to set the operating point.
2I4.full: Comparing amplifier configurations, and the characteristics of classes A, AB, B and C.

2I5.intermediate: How a transistor keeps a tuned circuit ringing, and where crystals beat variable oscillators.
2I5.full: The feedback an oscillator needs to keep itself going.

2I6.intermediate: An integrated circuit packs many devices onto one chip and gives you a whole function.

2J1.foundation: Cells and batteries, and where the energy in them comes from.
2J1.intermediate: Different chemistries give different voltages. Capacity is measured in ampere-hours.

2J2.intermediate: Half wave, full wave and bridge rectifiers, and how each one turns AC into DC.
2J2.full: Stabilising circuits, and how they hold the output steady when the load changes.

2J3.intermediate: A reservoir capacitor fills the gaps between rectifier pulses and smooths what comes out.
2J3.full: Peak inverse voltage, and choosing a diode that will survive it.

2J4.intermediate: Linear power supplies, and how they stack up against switch mode ones.
2J4.full: How a switch mode supply works, at block diagram level.

3A1.foundation: What a transmitter is for, and what modulation means.

3A2.foundation: Modulation is how the audio gets onto the radio carrier.
3A2.intermediate: Depth of modulation on AM, and the difference between wide and narrow band FM.
3A2.full: Modulation index, and how it decides the number of FM sidebands.

3A3.foundation: Modulate a carrier and you create sidebands either side of it.
3A3.intermediate: SSB throws away the carrier and one sideband, and why that is worth doing.

3A4.foundation: Recognising audio, a carrier, AM, FM and CW from the shapes they make.

3B1.foundation: The stages of a simple transmitter, and the order the signal passes through them.
3B1.intermediate: Block diagrams for CW, AM, SSB and FM transmitters.
3B1.full: Transmitters that mix their way up to the final frequency.

3C1.foundation: The oscillator decides your transmit frequency, so setting it wrong puts you off band.
3C1.intermediate: Crystal oscillators and VFOs, and what each one is good at.
3C1.full: Why drift matters, and what you can do to keep it small.

3C2.intermediate: What keeps an oscillator steady: solid construction, screening, and a clean supply.

3C3.intermediate: Direct digital synthesis, and generating a signal from numbers.
3C3.full: The phase locked loop synthesiser, and the job each stage does in the loop.

3D1.full: Frequency multipliers use harmonics to reach frequencies above the oscillator itself.

3E1.foundation: The microphone amplifier lifts your voice to the level the modulator needs.
3E1.intermediate: A balanced modulator gives you both sidebands and kills the carrier.
3E1.full: How AM, SSB and FM modulators work, and calculating the bandwidth each one takes.

3E2.intermediate: A sideband filter lets just one sideband through to the power amplifier.
3E2.full: Sideband filter circuits, and working out the frequencies involved.

3E3.intermediate: Put a varicap in an oscillator and you have frequency modulation.

3F1.foundation: The power amplifier lifts the signal to the level you actually transmit.
3F1.intermediate: Efficiency, and working out the RF you get out from the DC you put in.

3F2.full: Which modes need a linear amplifier, and how distortion makes harmonics and intermodulation.

3F3.foundation: The power amplifier needs a matched load. The wrong antenna can damage it.
3F3.full: The parts of a PA stage, and what each one contributes.

3F4.full: How mode and speech processing change the rating your PA needs, through peak to average power.

3F5.full: Automatic level control and the manual power knob, and what each is protecting.

3G1.foundation: Too much modulation distorts your signal and splashes into the channels next door.
3G1.full: Over-modulation makes audio harmonics, and those widen what you transmit.

3G2.intermediate: Oscillators, mixers and amplifiers all throw off harmonics of the frequency they work at.
3G2.full: Over-driving the PA widens your signal too, including when you drive an external amplifier.

3G3.intermediate: A filter passes some frequencies and blocks others. Where each type earns its place.
3G3.full: Avoiding harmonics in the first place, and what else a transmitter can radiate.

3G4.intermediate: Key a CW transmitter too sharply and the clicks spread either side of you.
3G4.full: Parasitic and self-oscillation, and how to cure them.

3G5.intermediate: What causes chirp, and how to get rid of it.
3G5.full: How a synthesiser can end up somewhere you did not intend, and how to stop it transmitting there.

3H1.foundation: What a receiver is for, and what demodulation means.

3H2.foundation: The stages of a simple receiver, and the order the signal passes through them.
3H2.intermediate: The crystal set and the direct conversion receiver, and what each stage does.

3H3.intermediate: Sensitivity, and what a very strong signal does to a receiver that cannot cope.
3H3.full: Intermodulation from overload, and how it buries the signal you were listening to.

3H4.intermediate: Selectivity, and the limits on rejecting what sits just outside your bandwidth.

3I1.intermediate: Why almost every receiver uses the superhet arrangement.
3I1.full: Single and double superhet block diagrams, and the job of each block.

3I2.intermediate: Mixing two frequencies gives you their sum and difference. One of those becomes the IF.
3I2.full: What a mixer does, and the other products it makes alongside the one you wanted.

3I3.intermediate: A fixed IF gives good selectivity, and mixing ahead of it lets you cover several bands.
3I3.full: Choosing a high or low IF, and why some receivers convert more than once.

3I4.full: The IF amplifier and IF transformer, and what happens when you couple two tuned circuits.

3I5.full: Phase noise, where it comes from, and why it is quoted in dBc/Hz.

3J1.full: The RF amplifier, and why bolting a preamp on the front does not always help.

3K1.foundation: The detector recovers your information and the audio stage makes it loud enough to hear.
3K1.intermediate: How a diode detector pulls audio off an AM signal, and why CW needs a beat oscillator.
3K1.full: AM, CW, SSB and FM demodulator circuits, and what the FM limiter is doing.

3L1.intermediate: Automatic gain control keeps the volume steady as signals rise and fall.
3L1.full: Where the AGC voltage comes from, and setting attack and decay to suit the signal.

3M1.foundation: An SDR digitises everything the antenna hears and does the rest in software.
3M1.intermediate: The Fourier transform sorts a jumbled signal into the separate parts that make it up.
3M1.full: Amplitude, frequency and phase modulation seen from the software side.

3M2.intermediate: The time domain and the frequency domain are two views of the same signal.
3M2.full: Two local oscillators 90 degrees apart give you I and Q.

3M3.intermediate: The blocks that make up an SDR, and how the signal moves between them.

3N1.full: A transceiver shares oscillators and filters between transmit and receive.

3N2.full: A transverter takes you to bands your radio does not cover. Working out the frequencies.

4A1.foundation: Which cables suit RF, and why coax is the usual choice.
4A1.intermediate: A balanced feeder carries equal and opposite currents, so the fields around it cancel.

4A2.foundation: Feeders lose signal, and they lose it on receive as well as transmit.
4A2.intermediate: Twin feeder against coax, and what a loss in dB means for the power that arrives.

4A3.intermediate: Characteristic impedance, and how the conductor size and spacing decide it.
4A3.full: Velocity factor, and why a cut length of cable is shorter than free space suggests.

4B1.foundation: Why you need a balun between coax and a dipole.
4B1.intermediate: Choke baluns, and how they are put together.
4B1.full: Transformer, sleeve and choke baluns, and the 1:1 and 4:1 circuits.

4C1.foundation: An antenna turns electrical signals into radio waves, and sets their polarisation.

4C2.foundation: Radiation patterns, and the polar diagrams of a dipole and a Yagi.
4C2.intermediate: Front to back ratio, beamwidth, and the fact that patterns are three dimensional.

4C3.foundation: Antenna gain comes from pointing the radiation somewhere rather than everywhere.

4C4.foundation: Gain quoted against an antenna that radiates equally in all directions, and what EIRP means.
4C4.intermediate: The isotropic radiator as a reference, and calculating EIRP from it.

4C5.foundation: At VHF and UHF, both ends want the same polarisation.
4C5.intermediate: Angle of radiation, and why a long path wants a low one.

4C6.foundation: The feed point, and the impedance it shows at the frequency the antenna was cut for.
4C6.intermediate: How feed point impedance ties together the current and the voltage at the antenna.

4D1.foundation: Recognising the dipole, ground plane, Yagi, end fed wire and 5/8 wave antennas.
4D1.intermediate: The three elements of a Yagi, and what the reflector and director each do.
4D1.full: Working out antenna lengths, including the end correction that makes them shorter.

4D2.intermediate: A trap is a parallel tuned circuit that lets one antenna work on more than one band.
4D2.full: Current and voltage along a dipole and a ground plane, and the impedance you feed them at.

4E1.foundation: The antenna has to suit the frequency you are using.
4E1.intermediate: The reflected wave meets the forward wave, and together they make a standing wave.
4E1.full: What SWR measures, and how it is worked out.

4E2.foundation: What an SWR meter is telling you.
4E2.full: Return loss, and why a low SWR on its own does not prove the antenna is any good.

4E3.full: Feeder loss flatters the SWR you read at the shack. At the antenna it is worse.

4F1.foundation: Use an antenna off frequency and the match changes. What that does to the transmitter.
4F1.intermediate: A matching unit gives the transmitter the impedance it was designed to see.
4F1.full: How a matching unit cancels reactance, and what it does and does not fix.

4F2.full: A quarter wave of feeder used as an impedance transformer.

4G1.foundation: Choosing the right RF connectors, and getting the braid connected properly.
4G1.intermediate: In a properly terminated coax the RF field stays inside the cable.

5A1.foundation: Radio waves travel in straight lines, and they refract, diffract and reflect.
5A1.full: In free space the power spreads out by an inverse square law.

5A2.foundation: VHF and UHF usually pass straight through the ionosphere and stay in the troposphere.
5A2.intermediate: Ground wave, space wave and sky wave, and what skip distance and the dead zone mean.

5A3.intermediate: A radio wave carries an electric field and a magnetic field at right angles to each other.
5A3.full: The E and H fields in phase and square to the direction of travel, and power flux density.

5B1.foundation: The ionosphere is layers of ionised gas, 70 to 400km up, made by the sun.
5B1.intermediate: What ionises those layers, and how they sit above one another.
5B1.full: What solar flares and sunspots do to propagation.

5B2.foundation: HF signals bend back in the ionosphere, and that is what lets you work the world.
5B2.intermediate: Ionisation changes with the hour, the season, and the eleven year sunspot cycle.
5B2.full: Critical frequency, and the highest frequency that will still come back to you.

5B3.intermediate: The F2 layer gives the longest hops, and several hops take you further still.
5B3.full: Near vertical incidence sky wave, and when you would want it.

5B4.intermediate: The D layer soaks up the lower frequencies by day and fades away at night.
5B4.full: The ionosphere can twist the polarisation of a wave on its way through.

5B5.intermediate: The 24 and 28MHz bands sometimes get the same lift that VHF does.

5C1.foundation: Hills cast radio shadows, buildings weaken signals, and range shrinks as frequency rises.

5C2.foundation: Heavy rain, hail and snow all eat into signals at UHF and above.

5C3.foundation: Height, gain, a clear path and power all set your VHF range. Height beats power.
5C3.intermediate: Multipath, where a signal reflected off a building or aircraft arrives alongside the direct one.
5C3.full: Bouncing signals off the moon, and why that needs everything working in your favour.

5D1.full: Galactic noise, which is random noise arriving from outside the atmosphere.

5D2.full: The link budget: power, feeder loss, antenna gain and path loss, added up end to end.

9A1.intermediate: Setting a multimeter to the right range and polarity before you connect it to anything.
9A1.full: Multiplier resistors and shunts, and how the meter itself disturbs the circuit you are measuring.

9A2.intermediate: A voltmeter goes across the circuit and an ammeter goes in line with it. Why that is.

9A3.intermediate: Analogue and digital displays, what each is better at, and reading both.
9A3.full: Tolerance, calibration and drift in frequency measurement, and the margin to allow.

9A4.full: Test gear has its own source and input impedance, and that changes the reading you get.

9A5.intermediate: Using a voltmeter and an ammeter together to find the power going into a circuit.
9A5.full: Measuring RF power into a dummy load, and what peak envelope power means for SSB.

9A6.full: Crystal calibrators, frequency counters and standard frequency transmissions, and their limits.

9A7.full: What is inside an SWR meter, and how to read one with single, twin or crossed needles.

9A8.full: The oscilloscope, and reading frequency and voltage straight off the trace.

9A9.full: The spectrum analyser, and picking out the fundamental and its harmonics on screen.

9B1.intermediate: Decibels are a power ratio. Build any of them from 3dB and 10dB steps.
9B1.full: The decibel equations, including dBW, dBm, and voltage ratios in dBV.

9C1.intermediate: Reading the resistor colour code, the tolerance bands, and the E12 series.
9C1.full: Temperature shifts component values, and what that does to a tuned circuit.

9D1.intermediate: Thin metal screening cuts unwanted radiation, both out of a box and between stages inside it.

9E1.intermediate: What soldering actually is, and what it does to the joint.

9E2.intermediate: Solder melts at low temperature, and the flux in it stops oxide forming.

9E3.intermediate: Some metals take solder easily and others fight you.

9E4.intermediate: Cleaning and tinning the iron, and why you tin the wires before you join them.
